result.summary: Chiron's daughter Ocyrrhoe, inspired by prophecy, foretells the fates of the infant Æsculapius and of her father Chiron. Before she can say more, the Gods forbid her to speak and turn her into a mare, who is then called Enippe.

scenes.title: Ocyrrhoe prophesies over the infant
scenes.summary: Ocyrrhoe, seized by prophetic inspiration, sees the infant Æsculapius and foretells his healing powers, death and revival, and her father's painful death.
scenes.stakes: Ocyrrhoe risks divine anger by revealing the secrets of the Fates.

scenes.title: Ocyrrhoe becomes a mare
scenes.summary: Forbidden to say more, Ocyrrhoe laments her gift as her human form gives way. She turns into a mare and is renamed Enippe.
scenes.stakes: She loses her human shape and her voice.

characters.name: Ocyrrhoe
characters.description: prophetic daughter of Chiron and Chariclo, turned into a mare

characters.name: Æsculapius
characters.description: divine infant pupil, destined to be a healer

alias_notes.explanation: The new name Ocyrrhoe receives after becoming a mare.

notable_quotes.reason: Ocyrrhoe regrets her prophetic knowledge, summing up the cost of foreseeing the future.

analysis.text: Forbidden knowledge is punished: prophecy beyond what the Gods allow brings transformation, a recurring Ovidian pattern.
The change is told gradually, voice blurring into neighing, which makes the loss of humanity vivid.

fun_facts.text: The name Ocyrrhoe means 'swift-flowing', fitting her birth by a rapid stream, and Enippe suggests 'mare'.

language_notes.text: Æsculapius will raise a mortal from death and be struck down by Jove's thunderbolt; Jove is his grandsire, as father of Apollo.
Æsculapius becomes a corpse, then a god again; this refers to his death by thunderbolt and later deification as a god of medicine.
The serpent's blood is the poisonous blood of the Hydra, on the arrows of Hercules, which wounds Chiron accidentally.
The three Goddesses are the Fates, who spin, measure and cut the thread of each life.
Enippe means roughly 'horse-mare' in Greek; the name records her new form.

context_notes.text: The pupil is the infant Æsculapius, son of Apollo, who becomes the god of medicine.
Chariclo is a nymph, and mother of Ocyrrhoë. Chiron, the wise Centaur, was a famed teacher of heroes and healers.
Divine powers limit what prophets may reveal; Ocyrrhoë has revealed too much of the Fates' and Jove's plans.

literary_notes.text: Chiron, born immortal, will pray for death. His immortality becomes the source of his suffering.
Her gift of prophecy becomes the cause of her punishment, so she wishes she had never known the future.
The transformation is narrated as it happens, with the speaker feeling each change in her own body.
Her speech blurs between human words and a mare's sound, showing the change through the voice.
